progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From B6b (transcription): a gene is a stretch of DNA that codes for a polypeptide; mRNA is copied from the template strand and matches the coding strand with U in place of T. From B6c (translation): codons of three bases read in order from the start codon AUG, with no gaps; most amino acids have more than one codon; three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA, "U Are Away, U Are Gone, U Go Away"); the codon chart is read with mRNA codons; a polypeptide must fold to work. From B7: sickle cell (GAG to GUG, glutamate to valine at position 6; with two copies the haemoglobin forms fibres at low oxygen and cells sickle); a changed amino acid can, but need not, change a protein's shape and job (the snapdragon active-site case). From b01: a mutation is a change in base sequence and can make a new allele. From b02: base analogues mispair and intercalating chemicals add or skip a base. Not assumed: point mutation, substitution, insertion, deletion as named mutation types, silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift, reading frame.
progression.startsWith: Change one base in a coding sequence. The video opens: In the gene for one chain of haemoglobin, change one base in the sixth codon, and you can get sickle cell disease.
progression.stopsAfter: defining a point mutation and its three processes (substitution, insertion, deletion); explaining that a substitution within a coding codon changes that codon, which may give the same amino acid (silent, because the code is degenerate), a different amino acid (missense, sickle cell) or a stop codon (nonsense, beta-globin codon 39, chain cut short); explaining that an insertion or deletion of one base regroups every codon after it (frameshift), so most later amino acids change and an early stop often appears; explaining that adding or removing a multiple of three bases keeps the frame and adds or removes amino acids; explaining that the effect depends on type and position (near the start of a gene, in an active site), so "point" describes the scale of the change, not the size of the effect; applying this to an unseen classification of three mutant sequences with a chart excerpt, and to the cystic fibrosis three-base deletion against the Tay-Sachs four-base insertion.
progression.nextLesson: chromosomal mutations, changes to whole segments or numbers of chromosomes (route entry bio-m6-b04).

teaching.task: Every one of these changes is a single base, so why can one keep the same amino acid, one swap an amino acid, and one stop the protein?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why one base can leave the amino acid the same (the new codon names the same amino acid, 3); why it can swap an amino acid (the new codon names a different one, 4); why it can stop the protein (the new codon is a stop, so the ribosome halts, 5); why an insertion or deletion is different (the ribosome keeps reading in threes from the start, so every later codon is regrouped, 6); why three bases don't shift the frame (a whole codon's worth, 7); why position matters (how much of the chain lies after the change, 8). Visible case: one gene (beta-globin) carries all three substitution outcomes; one short message carries the frameshift and the in-frame deletion. Video advantage: the frame window rides along and the brackets visibly regroup; the bead chain changes bead by bead; the THE FAT CAT words regroup. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items with every given on screen. Reading load: three rows, at most about three other text items; the attempt 1 card is the densest frame and is the task itself.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Three single-base changes in one beta-globin gene give three different results (hook), so the question is why one base can matter so differently; point mutation and its three processes are named after a reading board shows DNA, mRNA and polypeptide together; silent, missense and nonsense are each shown on the same gene (codon change, chart lookup, then the name); one lost base regroups every codon after it before the word frameshift is used; THE FAT CAT ATE THE RAT shows the reading frame and the multiple-of-three exception, with its limit said; type and position decide the effect, so point describes the scale of the change, not the size of the effect. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback, then the decision rule hands off to chromosomal mutations.
teaching.openingDecision: In the gene for one chain of haemoglobin, change one base in the sixth codon, and you can get sickle cell disease. Change a different base in that same codon, and the amino acid stays the same. Change one base in codon thirty-nine, and the chain stops partway, causing a blood disorder called beta thalassaemia. Every one of these is a single base. So why are the results so different?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is a sequence item: a short normal mRNA, three mutant mRNAs (A, B, C) and a codon chart excerpt; for each mutant, name the type of point mutation and describe its effect on the polypeptide. A is silent, B is nonsense, C is a one-base deletion that shifts the frame. It tests reading the new codon on the chart and recognising a frameshift from the regrouped codons. 10c is an explain item on two real alleles: the cystic fibrosis allele with three bases deleted (one amino acid missing) and the Tay-Sachs allele with four bases inserted (changed from the insertion onwards and cut short); explain the difference. It tests the multiple-of-three rule as a cause, not a definition. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reason, short working where needed, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: "compare the causes, processes and effects of different types of mutation, including but not limited to:" with the examples "point mutation" and "chromosomal mutation". This video owns the point mutation half: processes (substitution, insertion, deletion), effects (silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift; type and position) and a one-clause recall of causes from b02 (copying mistakes, base analogues, chemicals that slide between bases). b04 owns the chromosomal half and the point against chromosomal comparison. Update the ledger row for B6-IQ1-02 (shared with b01 and b04) when this design passes review.

design.visualSystem: One reading board throughout, three aligned rows, so the student always sees DNA change, codon change and amino acid change together. (1) Bottom row "gene (DNA)": b01's `SlimStrand` (two thin lines with rungs, a soft gene band); a changed position is one amber rung with b01's `BaseSwap` callout showing the coding-strand base ("A to T"). No letter tiles. (2) Middle row "mRNA": the codons as clean typeset text in terracotta (B6b's mRNA colour), grouped in threes with a thin bracket under each codon and a small "5'" and "3'"; the changed letter is amber. Codons are text, as HSC papers print them, never tiles. (3) Top row "polypeptide": B6c's amino acid beads (muted warm, three-letter name printed on each), joined by short peptide links; a changed bead takes an amber ring. A small painted ribosome (`m5x-ribosome-v1.png`, flipped as in B6c) rides along the mRNA row as the reader in scenes 2, 5 and 6, with a three-base amber window under it showing the frame. Codon lookups use B6c's chart excerpt card (two to four rows, computed by the ported `codonToAA`), sliding in at the right and leaving when its scene ends. A fixed tag at the far left labels the three rows on first use and fades after scene 3. Real objects are painted: the red cells (sickle) and, from B7, the coded haemoglobin blob (four lobes, two "alpha", two "beta"). Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three text items on screen at once besides the three rows; each callout or tag fades when the next cue lands, and the chart card leaves when its lookup is done.
design.transitionPlan: The reading board (gene, mRNA, polypeptide rows) stays on screen throughout: the hook's three results become chips, the board resets to a neutral message for the three processes, then returns to beta-globin codon 6 for silent and missense and slides along the gene band to codon 39 for nonsense; the ribosome rides the mRNA row with its three-base window for the stop and the frameshift; the board clears to one word line for THE FAT CAT and to a long gene band for what decides the effect; memory lines write on beside the bead icons; each attempt clears the board and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and fills the answer rows one point at a time; the step chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.

(2) On "Four isn't a multiple of three" "four bases inserted" underlines; four amber positions slide into the right row and every bracket after them regroups, the beads after it turning amber; on "a stop codon soon appears" a grey stop bar closes the right row early (line: "4 is not a multiple of 3: frameshift, early stop"). (3) On "only affects the amino acids where it happens" the chip "each change only affects the amino acids where it happens" writes on and takes a grey scribble cross. Settle on the model answer for about a second.
